system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 7: MODULE 5 - MORE ADVANCED ARRANGING TECHNIQUES

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 7 — MODULE 5 - MORE ADVANCED ARRANGING TECHNIQUES

_Pages 241-270._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## back cycling band context warning

> Note that this technique (like the other substitutions we have covered) won’t necessarily work well if
> you are playing in a band as the changes may clash with the original chord chart the other players are
> working off. But it’s a very effective reharmonization technique for solo jazz guitar arrangements.

**Significance (p. 243).** Critical performance-context rule about when back cycling is appropriate.

## common tone substitution rule

> Melodic common tone substitution rule: substitute any chord for another chord, as long as
> the new chord has a note in common with it that you use as the melody note on top.

**Significance (p. 247).** Core definitional rule for the common tone substitution technique.

## later-song placement of complex substitutions

> For that reason, it may be desirable to add these kinds of substitutions a bit later in the song form

**Significance (p. 246).** Structural-placement rule for extreme harmonic substitutions, balancing innovation with listener comprehension.

## swapping melody for licks/phrases

> Here we get to experiment with swapping out the original melody with our own single lines and
> improvised chord phrases.

**Significance (p. 248).** Introduces the technique of replacing written melody with improvised material.

## when to substitute licks for melody

> Whenever you get a jazz chart with a melodic figure that repeats (e.g. a repeat of an A section) - this
> can be a good place to use this technique.

**Significance (p. 248).** Specifies the structural trigger — a repeated melodic figure — that signals an appropriate moment to substitute a lick or chord phrase.

## minor ii V lick substitution

> You can see there is a minor ii V i progression at that point (Bm7b5 - E7(b9) - Am7), so you can use
> a minor ii V i jazz lick in the place of the melody at this point.

**Significance (p. 250).** Demonstrates the harmonic reasoning for matching a specific lick type to an underlying progression.

## Joe Pass rubato technique

> Joe Pass would play these spontaneous phrases with a high degree of rubato - pushing and pulling
> the tempo for dramatic effect:

**Significance (p. 251).** Names a specific expressive technique — rubato as dramatic device — associated with the model performer.

## metronome practice method

> Practice your arrangement with a metronome as follows:
>
> e Have the metronome click on every beat.
> e Then try the metronome clicking on beats 1 and 3 only.
> e Then have a go with the metronome on beats 2 and 4 only.
>
> The final version is most desirable for jazz as it helps give the music more of a swing.

**Significance (p. 252).** Gives a three-stage progressive metronome practice method with a clear rationale for the final stage.

## bar-by-bar practice method

> Instead, methodically work through just 1 or 2 bars per session. Spend time slowly practicing the
> fingering and carefully checking the notes are accurate and that everything is moving comfortably
> under your fingers.
>
> When 1-2 bars are flowing and feel good under the hands, move to the next 2 bars in your next
> session and so on, gradually learning the arrangement one step at a time.

**Significance (p. 253).** Prescribes a concrete, incremental practice unit (1–2 bars per session) and the criterion for advancement.

## arrangement vs. performance split

> Arranging a chord melody is only 50% of the work - the other 50% is turning your arrangement
> into a great performance on your guitar.

**Significance (p. 252).** Framing rule resetting expectations about the scope of preparation required.

## back cycling substitution rule

> Back cycling substitution rule - you can add chords to the chord progression of a song based
> on the ‘back cycle’, i.e. the circle of fourths.

**Significance (p. 243).** Explicit definitional rule for the back cycling technique.

## solo guitar rhythm pitfall

> Lagging too far behind the beat gives the whole arrangement a ‘sleepy’ feel which can result in a
> lackluster performance.

**Significance (p. 252).** Identifies the specific rhythmic pitfall unique to unaccompanied solo guitar.

CHAPTER FILE>>>
